title: Fermat's Two-Square Theorem via Gaussian Integers
description: Proves Fermat's two-square theorem: a prime p is a sum of two squares iff p = 2 or p ≡ 1 (mod 4). The forward direction uses a ZMod 4 decidability argument (squares are 0 or 1 mod 4, so their sum is never 3). The backward direction uses Mathlib's Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq. Also establishes the Gaussian integer connection: inert primes (p ≡ 3 mod 4) are simultaneously prime in ℤ[i] and inexpressible as sums of two squares — both facts from the same mod-4 obstruction.

overview.historicalContext: Fermat stated in 1640 (in a letter to Mersenne) that a prime p is expressible as a sum of two integer squares iff p = 2 or p ≡ 1 (mod 4). Despite claiming a proof, Fermat never published one. The first complete proof was given by Euler in 1747, using Fermat's method of infinite descent. In 1832, Gauss gave a conceptually cleaner proof using Gaussian integers ℤ[i]: p splits in ℤ[i] iff p = 2 or p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and splitting means p = N(π) = π·π̄ where π = a + bi gives p = a² + b². The mod-4 obstruction for primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) is elementary: squares are 0 or 1 mod 4, so their sum is at most 2, never 3. This is one of the oldest and most elegant results in number theory, connecting quadratic residues, Gaussian integers, and the arithmetic of ℤ[i].
overview.problemStatement: Does Fermat's two-square theorem follow directly from the Gaussian integer framework formalized in BezoutIdentityOQ02OQ01OQ02OQ02? Specifically: prove that for a prime p, the existence of integers a, b with a² + b² = p is equivalent to p = 2 or p ≡ 1 (mod 4).
overview.proofStrategy: The proof has two directions. Forward (sum → mod 4): assume a² + b² = p; cast to ZMod 4; since squares in ZMod 4 are only 0 or 1 (checked by fin_cases + decide over all 16 pairs), their sum is 0, 1, or 2, never 3; so p ≢ 3 (mod 4). Backward (mod 4 → sum): for p = 2, exhibit 1² + 1² = 2; for p ≡ 1 (mod 4), use Mathlib's Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq which requires only p % 4 ≠ 3 and [Fact p.Prime].
keyInsights: The mod-4 obstruction is decidable: all 16 pairs (a, b) in ZMod 4 × ZMod 4 satisfy a² + b² ≠ 3. This is the same ZMod 4 technique used in the parent proof (BezoutIdentityOQ02OQ01OQ02OQ02) to prove inert_prime — so the impossibility direction of the two-square theorem and the primality of inert primes in ℤ[i] have identical proofs.

The theorem unifies two perspectives: (1) number-theoretic (p is a sum of two squares iff it is not ≡ 3 mod 4), and (2) Gaussian-algebraic (p splits in ℤ[i] iff p = 2 or p ≡ 1 mod 4). The Lean proof explicitly connects both via inert_prime_not_sum_sq.

Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq in Mathlib requires [Fact p.Prime] as a typeclass instance, following Mathlib's convention of using Fact for global primality hypotheses. This is why the backward direction of fermat_two_square uses haveI : Fact p.Prime := ⟨hp⟩.

The integer form (fermat_two_square_int) reduces to the ℕ form via natAbs: a² = (a.natAbs)² for any integer a (using Int.natAbs_sq). This symmetry — that sign doesn't matter for squares — reflects the fact that the sum-of-squares question is purely about positive values.

The result split_prime_sum_sq makes the connection explicit: if a Gaussian integer z has norm.natAbs = p (prime) and is not a unit, then its real and imaginary parts give p = z.re.natAbs² + z.im.natAbs². This is the core of the Gaussian integer proof of Fermat's theorem.

sections.mathContext: Fermat's two-square theorem: $p = a^2 + b^2$ (prime) $\iff$ $p = 2$ or $p \equiv 1 \pmod{4}$. Imports `Mathlib.NumberTheory.SumTwoSquares` for `Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq`.

sections.title: Part 1: Mod-4 Obstruction
sections.summary: sq_mod4_cases: squares in ZMod 4 are 0 or 1 (by fin_cases). sum_sq_ne_three: sum of two squares in ZMod 4 is never 3 (by decide). not_sum_sq_of_mod4_eq_three: the main obstruction theorem using ZMod 4 casting.
sections.mathContext: For any $x \in \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$, $x^2 \in \{0, 1\}$ (checked by cases: $0^2=0, 1^2=1, 2^2=0, 3^2=1$). Hence $a^2 + b^2 \in \{0,1,2\}$, never 3. If $p \equiv 3 \pmod{4}$, cast $a^2+b^2=p$ to $\mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}$ via `congr_arg Nat.cast`, apply `ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff` to get $(p : \mathbb{Z}/4\mathbb{Z}) = 3$, contradiction.

sections.summary: Positive examples: 2 = 1²+1², 5 = 1²+2², 13 = 2²+3², 17 = 1²+4², 29 = 2²+5². Negative examples: 3, 7, 11 are not sums of two squares.
sections.mathContext: Primes $\equiv 1 \pmod 4$: 5, 13, 17, 29, 37, ... Primes $\equiv 3 \pmod 4$: 3, 7, 11, 19, 23, ... The density of each is 1/2 among all primes (Dirichlet's theorem). Each positive example is verified by `norm_num`; each negative example uses `not_sum_sq_of_mod4_eq_three`.

conclusion.summary: Fermat's two-square theorem is proved with 0 sorries and 0 axioms. The forward direction uses a decidable mod-4 obstruction (same ZMod 4 technique as the parent's inert_prime proof). The backward direction uses Mathlib's Nat.Prime.sq_add_sq. The Gaussian integer connection is made explicit via inert_prime_not_sum_sq and split_prime_sum_sq.
conclusion.implications: This proof demonstrates that the mod-4 obstruction — central to both Fermat's two-square theorem and the inert prime classification in ℤ[i] — can be handled mechanically by `decide` in ZMod 4. The same pattern applies to other sum-of-squares results: e.g., p = a² + 2b² iff p = 2 or p ≡ 1,3 (mod 8), using ZMod 8 decidability. The explicit connection between Gaussian integer splitting and sum-of-squares is a clean example of how algebraic number theory makes classical number theory transparent.
openQuestions: Can the proof be extended to Gaussian integer splitting: prove that p splits in ℤ[i] iff p = 2 or p ≡ 1 (mod 4), completing both directions of the prime classification?
